analysis.one_liner: Taxes toxic chemicals to fund state programs that help people living near polluting facilities relocate or clean up their neighborhoods.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to three House committees and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a trust fund, paid for by higher federal taxes on toxic chemicals and by ending tax exemptions on imported oil, to give states money for two purposes: helping people who live within five miles of major polluting facilities move away, and cleaning up areas contaminated by those facilities. Grants could also be used to buy property for or from those residents, with priority going to those living closest. The bill never moved past its initial referral to committees and died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People living within five miles of major industrial polluters — refineries, chemical plants, and Superfund-listed sites — would gain a path to move away from pollution or have their neighborhoods cleaned up, with money coming from taxes on the chemical and oil industries rather than from taxpayers generally. Environmentally-focused nonprofits and universities would gain a funding stream to run those projects.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a For Communities Trust Fund, funded by chemical excise taxes, to award grants to states for helping people living within five miles of major polluting facilities relocate away from them.
The same fund can pay to protect or clean up areas contaminated by hazardous air pollutants or hazardous substance releases from those facilities.
Grants could buy property for or from residents near designated facilities, and states must give priority to people living closest to the facility.

Pays for the program by increasing excise taxes on listed toxic chemicals (for example $11.35 per ton on benzene and ethylene), adjusted for inflation, and removes tax exemptions for imported crude oil and petroleum products.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and importers would pay higher per-ton excise taxes on dozens of listed substances, including benzene, mercury, and arsenic, and importers of crude oil and petroleum products would lose tax exemptions. Some of those costs could be passed on in prices for fuels and industrial goods.

drawbacks.text: Grants go only to environmentally-focused nonprofits and institutions of higher education, not directly to residents, so families near polluted sites depend on those organizations applying on their behalf.

Relocation money is capped at people living within five miles of a designated facility, and states decide how to prioritize, so neighbors just outside the line or without a nonprofit advocate could be left out.
Raising chemical excise taxes raises the input costs of chemical manufacturers and industrial users, a cost they could pass on in prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is real and targeted: people living next to polluting facilities would gain a funded path to relocate or to have their neighborhoods cleaned up, with the money coming from taxes on the chemicals linked to the harm. The design has some soft spots — grants flow through nonprofits and universities rather than directly to residents, and states control prioritization — but nothing in the record suggests a serious offsetting cost. The bill's fate was decided by inaction: it was referred to three committees and never advanced, and died when the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it expired when the term of Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 13, 2021 and referred to three committees: Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure.

It was subsequently referred to three subcommittees — Health, Environment and Climate Change, and Water Resources and Environment — but no committee or subcommittee ever held a markup or reported it out.
It received no floor vote and no further action through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
The bill ended with zero cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers, oil and gas importers, and industrial facilities near fenceline communities were spared the new taxes and the relocation and cleanup programs, while residents of those communities remain exposed.

for.name: Rep. Cedric L. Richmond
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to fund relocation and cleanup for communities near polluting facilities; it was his only action on it.

against.name: House committee leadership (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure)
against.role: Chairs of the three referring committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there was no record of partisan support or opposition — only a single Democratic sponsor and committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill raises per-ton excise taxes on dozens of listed toxic chemicals (for example $11.35 per ton on benzene and ethylene) and indexes them to inflation, and narrows exemptions under the related petroleum tax. Because those tax receipts fund relocation and cleanup grants, the industry's tax bill becomes the public's remedy.

The bill removes tax exemptions related to crude oil and petroleum products imported into the United States, subjecting them to the revived tax. This is a direct tax increase on a major industry to fund the trust fund.

industries.industry: Facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants or hold Superfund sites
industries.note: Designated facilities themselves are not directly taxed, but the bill funds programs that help their neighbors move away and pay for remediation of contamination their operations caused, increasing pressure and liability exposure around such sites.
Only nonprofits and institutions of higher education with an environmental mission can apply for the grants, making them the channel through which relocation and cleanup money reaches communities.
